Bayesian CCD and Response-Surface Inference

Source: vignettes/v31-bayesian-ccd-response-surfaces.Rmd
v31-bayesian-ccd-response-surfaces.Rmd

From an efficient matrix to posterior geometry

The previous vignette treated the experimental matrix as a pre-data object.

This vignette begins after responses have been observed.

The goal is not merely to fit a quadratic regression and print coefficients.

A Bayesian response-surface workflow should propagate coefficient uncertainty into the shape of the surface, stationary point, canonical classification, bounded optimum, economic optimum, and response at those optima.

The sequential response-surface logic introduced by Box and Wilson remains the conceptual foundation (Box and Wilson 1951).

Classical rsm workflows provide important reference concepts such as coded variables, canonical analysis, steepest ascent, and ridge analysis (Lenth 2009).

Version 1.1.0 expresses these quantities as posterior objects whenever possible.

Learning objectives

After this vignette, the reader should be able to:

  • create a first- or second-order Bayesian RSM specification;
  • choose the native teaching engine or an optional Stan route;
  • define scientifically defensible priors;
  • inspect posterior coefficients without confusing them with the final scientific decision;
  • perform canonical analysis draw by draw;
  • interpret posterior probabilities of maximum, minimum, saddle, and flat/ridge geometry;
  • estimate bounded biological optima;
  • estimate economic optima under explicit prices and costs;
  • trace steepest-ascent or descent paths;
  • inspect ridge paths;
  • propagate uncertainty into multiresponse desirability;
  • distinguish a stationary point from an operational optimum.

1. Teaching CCD data

The package includes a frozen simulated two-factor agronomic CCD.

library(bayesAgriFlow)
d <- bayes_teaching_data("ccd")
head(d)

The natural factors are nitrogen N and phosphorus P.

The design also contains coded_N and coded_P.

The response is simulated yield.

It is teaching data, not empirical evidence.

2. Fit on coded coordinates

For geometric interpretation, coded coordinates are often preferable.

des <- bayes_rsm(
  data = d,
  response = "yield",
  factors = c("coded_N", "coded_P"),
  order = 2,
  family = "gaussian"
)
des

The second-order basis contains an intercept, two linear terms, two pure quadratic terms, and their interaction.

3. Inspect the plan 

plan <- bayes_plan(des)
plan

For a Gaussian fixed-design RSM, the default plan can use the native conjugate teaching engine.

This keeps examples lightweight and provides direct posterior coefficient draws.

A confirmatory analysis can instead use the optional brms/Stan path with explicit priors and computation controls.

4. Prior predictive reasoning

Before looking only at the posterior, ask whether the coefficient prior implies plausible responses over the design region.

pr <- bayes_prior(
  strategy = "regularizing",
  coefficient_scale = 1.5,
  intercept_scale = 3
)
pp <- bayes_prior_predictive(
  des,
  prior = pr,
  draws = 500,
  seed = 20260826
)
pp$summary

A prior that routinely generates impossible agronomic yields should be revised before being defended as scientifically regularizing.

5. Native posterior fit 

fit <- bayes_fit(
  des,
  engine = "native",
  prior = pr,
  draws = 4000,
  seed = 20260826
)
fit

6. Posterior coefficient summaries 

bayes_summary(fit)
bayes_effects(fit)

The coefficient table is only one representation of the response surface.

Linear and quadratic coefficients depend on coding and origin.

The posterior surface and its derived geometry are usually more directly related to agronomic questions.

7. Posterior prediction 

grid <- expand.grid(
  coded_N = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 15),
  coded_P = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 15)
)
pred <- bayes_predict(fit, grid)
head(pred$summary)

The prediction interface rebuilds internal RSM basis columns automatically from the factor values supplied in newdata.

Users should not have to construct hidden quadratic columns manually.

8. Posterior predictive check 

bayes_pp_check(fit)

A design can be excellent while the fitted quadratic surface is inadequate.

Posterior predictive checks address the model-data relationship, not the pre-experimental geometry alone.

9. Canonical representation

For a conventional second-order surface in coded coordinates:

y=β0+bTx+xTBx. y = \beta_0 + b^T x + x^T Bx.

The stationary point solves:

b+2Bx=0. b + 2Bx = 0.

When B is nonsingular:

xs=−12B−1b. x_s = -\frac{1}{2}B^{-1}b.

A classical analysis computes this from one coefficient estimate.

Version 1.1.0 computes it for posterior draws.

10. Posterior canonical analysis 

can <- bayes_rsm_canonical(
  fit,
  level = 0.95,
  max_draws = 1000
)
can

The summary gives posterior intervals for stationary-point coordinates.

The object also stores the draw-level stationary points and eigenvalues.

11. Surface classification

The eigenvalues of B characterize local curvature.

For each posterior draw:

  • all negative implies a local maximum;
  • all positive implies a local minimum;
  • mixed signs imply a saddle;
  • near-zero eigenvalues imply ridge-like or locally flat geometry under the selected tolerance.

The output therefore reports probabilities rather than one categorical label.

can$classification

A result such as P(maximum)=0.80 contains more information than simply printing “maximum”.

12. Stationary point versus bounded optimum

A stationary point can lie outside the experimental region.

It can also be a saddle.

For operational decisions, optimize over explicit feasible bounds.

opt <- bayes_rsm_optimum(
  fit,
  bounds = list(
    coded_N = c(-1.5, 1.5),
    coded_P = c(-1.5, 1.5)
  ),
  goal = "max",
  max_draws = 500
)
opt

13. Draw-by-draw optimization

bayes_rsm_optimum() optimizes each retained posterior coefficient draw.

Consequently, uncertainty in coefficients propagates to uncertainty in optimum coordinates and response.

The result contains:

  • optimum-coordinate draws;
  • response-at-optimum draws;
  • posterior interval summaries;
  • boundary probability.

14. Boundary probability 

opt$boundary_probability

A high probability of a boundary optimum is scientifically important.

It can indicate that the chosen region does not contain the response maximum or that the fitted surface keeps increasing toward a boundary.

It should not be hidden by printing only the median optimum.

15. Natural-scale optimization

The same model can be fitted on natural factors when decisions need direct units.

des_nat <- bayes_rsm(
  d,
  response = "yield",
  factors = c("N", "P"),
  order = 2
)
fit_nat <- bayes_fit(des_nat, draws = 3000, seed = 20260826)

opt_nat <- bayes_rsm_optimum(
  fit_nat,
  bounds = list(
    N = c(40, 200),
    P = c(20, 100)
  ),
  max_draws = 400
)
opt_nat

Numerical conditioning should be checked when fitting directly on natural scales.

Coding is often preferable for geometry, with a documented transformation back to field units.

16. Economic optimum

The biological maximum need not maximize profit.

eco <- bayes_rsm_economic_optimum(
  fit_nat,
  bounds = list(
    N = c(40, 200),
    P = c(20, 100)
  ),
  output_price = 1200,
  input_costs = c(N = 5, P = 4),
  fixed_cost = 300,
  max_draws = 400
)
eco

Prices and costs are part of the decision model.

Changing them changes the economic optimum without changing the biological posterior surface.

17. Do not confuse utility with evidence

An economic optimum is not stronger statistical evidence.

A Bayes factor is not a profit measure.

A ROPE is not an economic loss function unless it has explicitly been defined that way.

The package keeps estimation, evidence, prediction, and decision layers separate.

18. Steepest ascent

When experimentation is sequential and the current region is far from an optimum, a first-order local path can guide the next region.

path <- bayes_rsm_steepest(
  fit,
  direction = "ascent",
  start = c(0, 0),
  step = 0.20,
  n_steps = 8
)
path

The path direction uses the posterior-median gradient at the starting point.

Posterior response intervals are then propagated along the path.

19. Steepest descent 

bayes_rsm_steepest(
  fit,
  direction = "descent",
  step = 0.15,
  n_steps = 5
)

This can be relevant when the response is something undesirable, such as disease severity or environmental loss.

20. Ridge analysis

A stationary point may be poorly determined along a nearly flat direction.

Ridge analysis examines best predicted response over shells at fixed coded radius.

ridge <- bayes_rsm_ridge(
  fit,
  radii = seq(0, 1.2, by = 0.2),
  goal = "max",
  directions = 1000,
  seed = 20260826
)
ridge

The implementation uses a reproducible directional search.

The returned response intervals propagate posterior coefficient uncertainty at the selected ridge point.

21. Ridge is not a confidence region

A ridge path and a credible region answer different questions.

The ridge path asks where the response is best under a fixed-radius constraint.

A credible region asks which parameter or optimum locations remain plausible under the posterior.

22. Student-t response surfaces

When continuous responses contain heavier tails than a Gaussian model can reasonably represent, specify:

des_t <- bayes_rsm(
  d,
  "yield",
  c("coded_N", "coded_P"),
  family = "student"
)
bayes_plan(des_t)

This routes to the optional brms/Stan backend.

The experimental design does not change merely because the likelihood changes.

23. CmdStan computation 

compute <- bayes_compute(
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  n_cpus = 8,
  chains = 4,
  parallel_chains = 4,
  seed = 20260826
)

fit_stan <- bayes_fit(
  des,
  engine = "brms",
  compute = compute
)

Runtime MCMC diagnostics remain mandatory before scientific interpretation.

24. Diagnostics before optimization

A posterior optimum is only as defensible as the fitted posterior model.

Check:

  • R-hat;
  • effective sample size;
  • divergences;
  • treedepth warnings;
  • posterior predictive adequacy;
  • sensitivity to priors;
  • sensitivity to model form.

Optimization does not repair poor sampling or model misspecification.

25. Frequentist crosswalk

For teaching, the same fixed RSM formula can be fit with lm() through the package’s frequentist crosswalk.

bayes_compare_frequentist(fit)

The crosswalk does not determine whether the Bayesian analysis is accepted or rejected.

It helps students connect familiar least-squares coefficients with posterior quantities.

26. Multiresponse teaching data

Many agronomic decisions involve more than yield.

dm <- bayes_teaching_data("ccd_multiresponse")
head(dm)

The dataset includes simulated yield, protein, and lodging outcomes on a common CCD.

27. Fit response-specific surfaces 

fy <- bayes_fit(
  bayes_rsm(dm, "yield", c("coded_N", "coded_P")),
  draws = 2000
)
fp <- bayes_fit(
  bayes_rsm(dm, "protein", c("coded_N", "coded_P")),
  draws = 2000
)
fl <- bayes_fit(
  bayes_rsm(dm, "lodging", c("coded_N", "coded_P")),
  draws = 2000
)

These are separate response models.

For strongly correlated residual outcomes where joint covariance is scientifically essential, use the package’s multivariate modeling layer rather than assuming independence without discussion.

28. Desirability specifications

Suppose the goal is:

  • maximize yield;
  • target protein near 12 percent;
  • minimize lodging.
specs <- list(
  yield = list(type = "maximize"),
  protein = list(type = "target", target = 12),
  lodging = list(type = "minimize")
)

29. Posterior desirability optimum 

multi <- bayes_rsm_desirability(
  fits = list(yield = fy, protein = fp, lodging = fl),
  specs = specs,
  bounds = list(
    coded_N = c(-1.5, 1.5),
    coded_P = c(-1.5, 1.5)
  ),
  weights = c(yield = 2, protein = 1, lodging = 1),
  grid_n = 20,
  max_draws = 300
)
multi

The result is a distribution of optimal compromise locations rather than one deterministic desirability coordinate.

30. Weight sensitivity

Weights encode decision priorities.

They are not estimated scientific truths.

Repeat the analysis under plausible alternative weights and document whether recommendations change.

31. Model-form sensitivity

A second-order polynomial is a local approximation.

If posterior predictive checks reveal systematic lack of fit, compare scientifically plausible nonlinear, spline, or Gaussian-process alternatives already available in bayesAgriFlow.

Do not select a more flexible model solely because it produces a more attractive optimum.

32. Extrapolation

Optimization should default to the experimental region or a scientifically justified operational subset.

A mathematically calculated optimum far outside observed support is an extrapolation, not a new experimental fact.

33. Reporting the optimum

A useful report includes:

  • factor scale and coding;
  • model formula;
  • priors;
  • posterior diagnostics;
  • posterior predictive checks;
  • stationary-point distribution;
  • canonical classification probabilities;
  • bounded optimum distribution;
  • response at the optimum;
  • boundary probability;
  • economic assumptions when used;
  • sensitivity analyses.

34. Report an operating region when useful

Agronomic decisions often tolerate a range of nearly optimal factor combinations.

A narrow focus on a single coordinate can create false precision.

The posterior optimum cloud and decision utilities can be used to define a practical operating region in downstream analyses.

35. Reproducibility

Record package version, backend, seed, design matrix, priors, factor bounds, prices, costs, and optimization settings.

The result should be reproducible from code, not only from a contour screenshot.

Summary

Version 1.1.0 treats response-surface geometry as a posterior-derived quantity.

The design remains explicit, model uncertainty is propagated, and the stationary point is kept distinct from bounded and economic optima.

The next vignette returns to pre-experimental comparison and adds matrix-efficiency criteria, pseudoquadratic fertilizer models, Bayesian design information, assurance, and sequential augmentation.

Box, George E. P., and K. B. Wilson. 1951. “On the Experimental Attainment of Optimum Conditions.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological) 13 (1): 1–38. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1951.tb00067.x.
Lenth, Russell V. 2009. “Response-Surface Methods in r, Using Rsm.” Journal of Statistical Software 32 (7): 1–17. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v032.i07.
